Hormuz: Trump vows to sink Iranian tankers that try to run the blockade and threatens to strike Iran again after New Year

This weekend, Donald Trump warned that Iranian tankers trying to run the US blockade would end up “at the bottom of the sea” and said he was inclined to resume strikes after New Year if there is no deal. The United States hit a tanker near the blockade line. On Monday, Brent was holding around $92 [1][3][4][8].

The US president said he was inclined to resume strikes on Iran after New Year if negotiations fail [1][9]. Yet in early November, he had described the war as “practically over” in military terms [2].

Asked about the more than 14 tankers that Tehran is reportedly preparing at Kharg Island to run the blockade, according to the Iranian newspaper Hamshahri, he said: “They will all be at the bottom of the sea, like the Iranian navy” [3].
Nothing confirms that Tehran has ordered the convoy to set sail; an adviser to the NGO United Against Nuclear Iran calls the plan “almost impossible” and sees it as propaganda [3].

The United States struck a tanker carrying Iranian oil near its blockade line, Gulf News reported on Monday. The speaker of Iran's Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, is calling for “lasting deterrence” [4].

On Sunday, the British agency UKMTO reported an incident in the Gulf of Oman between a tanker and “military forces”, near the blockade line [5]. The same day, the TankerTrackers website showed that an Iranian tanker supposedly crossing the strait did not exist: its signal was fake [6][10].

On the diplomatic front, a Qatari delegation spent about two hours in Tehran on Friday evening. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says reopening Hormuz would be “not difficult” if Washington accepts “reasonable” conditions; Qatar and Pakistan are acting as mediators, with no formal negotiations at this stage [7].

At Monday's open, Brent was down 28 cents (0.30%) at $92.29, and WTI was at $83.26: falling stock markets, worried about artificial intelligence, weighed more than the weekend's attacks, including the Houthis' claim of a strike on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery [8].

The key takeaway: Washington and Tehran are hardening their tone just as Qatari mediation stalls, and Trump is setting a deadline for the first time, New Year, for a possible resumption of strikes [1][7].

The blockade aims to stop Iran from exporting its oil. If a convoy of tankers tried to force its way through, the US Navy would have to choose between letting it go and opening fire, with a risk of escalation in a strait through which a large share of the world's oil passes [3][4].
The fake tanker spotted by tracking websites points to an information war around the strait [6][10].

For now, markets are looking elsewhere: the International Energy Agency expects a global surplus of about 2 million barrels per day this quarter, which is keeping prices in check [9]. OPEC+ countries set their 2027 output on November 29 [9].

The price at the pump depends largely on Brent. As long as it stays around $92, there is no new spike, but a naval confrontation in Hormuz or a resumption of strikes in January could send it back up very quickly, and the cost of filling up your tank along with it.

Canada-US: a deal is “pretty close”, says Trump's negotiator, who faults Ottawa over its 49,000 Chinese electric cars

On Sunday, November 22, on Fox News, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington and Ottawa were “pretty close” to common ground on tariffs. But he criticized Canada's rapprochement with China, in particular the entry each year of 49,000 Chinese electric cars at reduced tariffs [1][2].
Interviewed on Fox News on Sunday, Jamieson Greer said the two countries were “pretty close to finding a landing zone”, meaning a compromise acceptable to each side [1][2].
He also described the negotiation as going “a bit backwards” because of Canada's new trade ties with China, a source of concern in Washington [1][2].

He is targeting Ottawa's decision to let in 49,000 Chinese electric cars a year at a reduced tariff, and its tariff cuts on Chinese vehicles, steel and aluminum [2]. Canada and China have also cut tariffs on products such as pork and seafood [5].
This concern is shared by lawmakers from both parties in Congress, according to Greer [6].

Canada is aiming for an interim arrangement by the end of the year: lower “232” tariffs (steel, aluminum, autos, lumber) and full removal of the “338” tariffs [1]. According to the Canadian press, however, Ottawa's chief negotiator has warned that several issues remain open [1][4].

On Thursday, November 19, minister Dominic LeBlanc gave an update to the advisory committee on Canada-US economic relations, its first meeting since the midterm elections. He warned against the idea that a Democratic majority in Congress would automatically settle the dispute [4].

Talks had collapsed in August, when Canada walked away in the face of last-minute US demands [2]. Canadian cars face 25% tariffs, and Donald Trump has threatened to raise them to 50% on January 1, 2027 [5].
The key takeaway: for the first time in weeks, a senior US official is talking about a deal within reach, but he attaches a political condition: that Canada distance itself from China [1][2].

The criticism is not new. On November 17, a Trump trade adviser had asked Mark Carney whether he was really threatening to “play China against the United States”, and called the auto talks between Ottawa and Beijing “offensive” [5].

The US calendar also matters. After their midterm victory, Democrats want to make repealing Trump's tariffs a priority when the new Congress sits in 2027 [8]. A Reuters/Ipsos poll shows that 62% of Americans support this, but the White House vows to stay the course [7].

Ottawa is therefore staying cautious: LeBlanc hopes for an arrangement before the end of 2026, without setting a rigid deadline [4]. The central issue remains autos, where the threat of tariffs doubling on January 1 is getting closer [5].
A new rule of the game in Washington: to get lower tariffs, an ally must limit its trade with China. Europe, which is also negotiating with Trump, could face the same condition.

AI crash: Beijing lets Chinese investors borrow more to buy stocks, but its markets slide again on Monday

The Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges announced on Saturday, November 22, that investors will soon be able to buy stocks on credit with less money down: the minimum deposit drops from 100% to 80% on November 30. Yet on Monday, the CSI 300 index lost 1.1% and Shanghai 1.5% [1][2][5].
With the approval of China's securities regulator (CSRC), the three exchanges are lowering the minimum “margin ratio”: the amount an investor must put up to borrow and buy stocks [1][2].
In practice, with the same deposit, you can now borrow more. The rule takes effect on November 30 and reverses a tightening decided in January [2].
The exchanges estimate that the measure could free up nearly 400 billion yuan in new funds. This is a theoretical maximum: they do not say how much will actually flow into the market [2][3].

They justify the move by a sharp drop in buying on credit, while overall investor leverage remains low [1]. Outstanding margin loans stand at around 2,200 billion yuan, compared with a peak of 3,000 billion at the end of June [2].
Shanghai and Shenzhen are also cutting some fees, and Shenzhen is publishing draft rules for market makers on ChiNext, its tech-stock board [3].
Yet on Monday, November 23, Chinese stocks opened lower: the weekend's easing did not reassure investors worried about the global AI crash and US chip restrictions [4].
In Asia, tech and semiconductor stocks were sold off again, amid doubts over AI valuations and the debt raised to fund data centers [5].
The key takeaway: Beijing is using credit to prop up its stock market, a sign that the fall in AI-related stocks worries it [1][7].

The slide has lasted for weeks. On October 22, the CSI 300 had already fallen into a “bear market”, more than 20% below its June peak, and the STAR 50 tech index had lost nearly 40% in six months [6]. By mid-November, the CSI 300 was down 14% since January [7].

Credit is a double-edged sword. In January, Beijing had tightened the rules to curb speculation; today it is doing the opposite [2]. Buying on credit amplifies gains when the market rises, but also losses when it falls.
The first test failed: on Monday, stocks fell despite the weekend's move [4]. If the decline continues, Beijing may have to announce further support measures [7].

If you have a fund invested in Chinese or Asian stocks, it may stay very volatile as long as doubts about AI persist. Beijing's measures show that the state wants to slow the decline, but they did not reverse the trend on Monday.

Brazil: lawmakers vote this Monday evening on Lula's savings plan without changing a comma, the last step before he signs it

Brazil's Chamber of Deputies is meeting in an extraordinary session this Monday, November 23, at 6 p.m. to vote on the Lula government's fiscal adjustment plan, already passed by the Senate. The rapporteur changed nothing: if approved, the bill, which is expected to bring in about 50 billion reais in 2027, goes straight to the president for signature [1][2][4].
The speaker of the Chamber, Hugo Motta, called an extraordinary session at 6 p.m. on a Monday, a day when deputies rarely vote [1][5]. Debates could run into Tuesday, November 24 [3][5].
The rapporteur, Mauro Benevides, kept the Senate text as is: if adopted, complementary bill PLP 299/2026 does not need to go back to the Senate and goes directly to Lula for signature [1][6].
An “urgency” request, which speeds up the vote, is on the agenda; it requires 257 votes [1][2].
The bill caps spending growth during periods of fiscal strain, cuts tax breaks granted to specific sectors by a uniform 10%, and limits the use of tax credits to offset other debts [1][4].

The current fiscal rule allows spending to grow by up to 2.5% above inflation each year [4]. The Senate rapporteur, Eduardo Braga, estimates the package's impact at about 50 billion reais in 2027 [3][4].

Deputies from the Workers' Party (PT), Lula's party, are pushing for adoption; the business federations CNI, Fiesp and Fiemg are worried, arguing that large companies will foot most of the bill [2][6].
Mansueto Almeida, an economist at the bank BTG Pactual, says the plan is “in the right direction”, but too small for the fiscal problem [7].
The key takeaway: this is the first major credibility test for the re-elected Lula in the eyes of the markets. Markets want savings voted into law, and fast [1][7].

The pressure is intense: on November 19, the central bank had to sell $1 billion to slow the real's slide, its first intervention of this kind since December 2024, and the dollar still ended at 5.93 reais [9][10]. According to market forecasts, inflation and interest rates are expected to rise further [7].

The decision not to change anything in the Senate text, which was wrapped up on November 18 [8], aims to avoid another round trip between the two chambers. But business groups are contesting the cut in tax breaks, and some economists consider the effort too modest to stabilize the debt [2][7].

Brazil is a giant in soybeans, coffee and sugar. If lawmakers reassure the markets, the real could stabilize; if they stumble, the currency could fall again, which moves global prices for these commodities and affects European companies operating in Brazil.

news.2026-11-23-philippines-marcos-econo: Philippines: sluggish growth, weak peso, drought: Marcos defends his economic team and contradicts Trump on “exclusive” purchases from the United States

Back from the APEC summit in China, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on November 22 defended his economic team, criticized over the slowdown, inflation and the weak peso. He blames the war with Iran. He also denied having promised Donald Trump to buy all of the country's oil and food from the United States [1][3][4].
Ferdinand Marcos Jr reaffirmed his confidence in his economic team, under fire for slowing growth, rising inflation and a weaker peso. He attributes these difficulties to the war with Iran [1].
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson rejected this explanation on November 23: according to him, other Southeast Asian countries, hit by the same crisis, are growing faster [2].

Donald Trump had claimed that the Philippines had committed to making the United States its sole source of agricultural products and energy. Marcos set the record straight: Manila wants more suppliers, not exclusive suppliers [3][4].
According to Marcos, US soybeans and some US wheat could make up for lost trade with Ukraine and Russia [3].

He said he was “puzzled” by the protests against Pax Silica, a US-led initiative, and insisted that “there is no agreement yet”. The National Union of Peoples' Lawyers (NUPL) says the remark is hard to take seriously and calls for the project to be rejected [5].
Congresswoman Leila de Lima is asking him to declare a state of calamity in areas hit by El Niño, where production losses have reached 288,424 tonnes [6].
The key takeaway: Marcos is caught between a struggling economy and a demanding American ally, as pressure mounts in Manila [1][3].
The president points to an external shock, the war with Iran. But the argument does not convince the opposition, which compares the country with neighbors hit by the same crisis [1][2].

With Trump, Marcos is seeking a balance. He wants to buy more American goods to improve trade relations, without locking himself into a single dependency that would deprive the country of lower prices elsewhere [3][4].

The El Niño-related drought adds a risk for agriculture and food prices, with nearly 290,000 tonnes of crops already lost [6]. The same phenomenon has pushed Fiji and Tonga to declare emergencies in recent days.
The Philippines show how the war with Iran spreads: more expensive energy, a weaker currency, slowing growth. For you, it is the same mechanism that weighs on fuel prices in Europe.

After the Nasdaq's worst week since 2020, Wall Street futures rebound 2% and gold recovers 2.3% overnight

Overnight from Sunday to Monday, November 23, futures on Wall Street indices rebounded about 2%, after a week in which the Nasdaq lost 10%, its worst since March 2020. Gold regained 2.3%, to around $3,620 an ounce. But analysts doubt the rebound will hold [1][2][3].

S&P 500 futures were up 1.9% and Nasdaq 100 futures 2.3% during Asian trading, according to Bloomberg [2]. Reuters reported +2% for the Nasdaq 100 and +1% for the S&P 500 at the very start of the session [1].

On Friday, November 20, the S&P 500 had fallen for the seventh session in a row and entered a “correction”, meaning 10% below its high [2]. The Nasdaq had dropped 5.3%, the S&P 500 3.7% and Nvidia 14% [5].
Over the week, the Nasdaq lost 10%, its biggest weekly drop since the Covid panic in March 2020, according to Reuters [1].
Spot gold rebounded about 2.3%, to around $3,620 an ounce [3]. It had ended Friday at $3,537.90, after a week at −9.5% on the Comex futures market, according to Goodreturns [4].

US Treasury futures fell, ending five sessions of gains: investors are seeking less safety [3]. The yen was the exception, with the dollar worth about 158.90 yen, in a quiet market as Japan was on holiday [3].
An analyst quoted by investingLive believes no trigger can turn this rebound into a lasting recovery without a change of course by central banks [3].
In Europe on Friday, the Euro Stoxx 50 had lost 2.81% and Germany's DAX 2.60% [5]. On Monday, PMI business activity indicators for the eurozone and the United States are due [9].

The key takeaway: after such a steep fall, a rebound is almost mechanical. Those who had bet on a decline lock in their gains by buying back, and buyers return at lower prices. One analyst noted that a rebound was likely after seven straight days of decline [3].

The cause of the fall has not gone away. The doubt is about AI: Nvidia lost about $500 billion in value in a single day on Friday [6], after Reuters reported an investigation by the US securities regulator, the SEC, into its accounting [7].

Gold is a textbook case. It is supposed to offer protection in a storm, but during the fall it was sold to raise cash, just like stocks [3]. Its rebound on Monday also reportedly reflects reduced bets on an imminent Fed rate hike [4].
AI debt is also a worry: in early November, Oracle raised $20 billion, including $10 billion in bonds at rates of 7% to 8.65%, to fund its data centers [8].

If you are looking at your stock savings after a week like this, don't rely on an overnight rebound: it can vanish during the day. Futures are only a foretaste of the open. What matters for a saver is a horizon of several years, not Monday's session.

How it works: futures, the stock market before the stock market

Wall Street opens at 3:30 p.m. Paris time. But futures on its indices, such as the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq 100, trade almost 24 hours a day. A futures contract is a commitment to buy or sell the index later at a price set today. Its price therefore takes the market's temperature before the open: on Sunday evening, Nasdaq 100 futures were up 2.3% [2]. Be careful: it is mostly large investors and traders who trade them, with lower volumes overnight. A rebound in futures can be confirmed at the open or disappear, depending on the day's news [3].

Chemicals: Switzerland's Clariant and the fund CD&R are negotiating to buy US-based Ashland for about $3.4 billion, with no premium

Swiss chemicals maker Clariant and US investment fund CD&R are in talks to buy US chemicals maker Ashland, Bloomberg revealed on Sunday, November 22. The all-cash offer would value Ashland at around $3.39 billion, close to its Friday share price, and therefore without the usual premium. A deal could come in the next few days [1][2].
Clariant, a Swiss specialty chemicals company, and CD&R, a US private equity firm, are in talks to buy Ashland, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg [1].
The offer would be paid entirely in cash and would value Ashland close to its share price on Friday, November 20 [1], or about $3.39 billion, according to Reuters [2].
A deal could be reached as early as the next few days. But the talks could still fall through, or another buyer could come forward, Bloomberg notes [1][3].
Ashland put itself up for sale in July, after an agreement with the activist fund Ancora, which considered the company undervalued [1].
In August, Ashland hired the banks Citigroup and Lazard to explore a sale. Four funds, Advent, Apollo, Carlyle and Standard Industries, also had contacts with the group [1].
According to Mergermarket, cited by the German website Dr. Web, Clariant on its own could run into competition authorities: that is one reason to team up with a fund [4].
Ashland and Clariant declined to comment; CD&R did not immediately respond [1].

The key takeaway: European chemicals companies are looking to grow while prices are low. Buying a competitor makes it possible to share plants, customers and costs. Teaming up with a fund means paying less on your own and splitting up the businesses afterward [1][4].

The most surprising thing is the price. Usually, the buyer pays a premium to convince shareholders to sell: Iceye offered 20% above the share price for Italy's Avio last week [5]. Here, the offer would be close to Friday's share price [1].

Why might Ashland's shareholders accept? The group has been looking for a buyer since July, under pressure from an activist fund [1]. After months of searching, the number of serious bidders matters more than the premium, especially when the stock market is nervous.
The deal also shows that takeovers are continuing despite the market storm: funds have plenty of money to invest, and prices are falling [1][6].

If you own shares in a company that could be bought, know that the rumor often makes the share price jump, but not always. Here, with no premium, there is almost nothing to gain for Ashland's shareholders. And a rumor is not a deal: talks can fall through.

How it works: the “control premium” in a takeover

When one company buys another, it has to convince thousands of shareholders to sell it their shares. To do so, it usually offers more than the share price: this is the control premium, often 20 to 40%. Example: Iceye's offer for Avio, at €41 per share, offered about 20% above the share price, and the stock jumped more than 13% [5]. The price rises toward the offer price without quite reaching it, because there is still a risk of failure. An offer with no premium, like the one under consideration for Ashland [1], is rare: it happens when the seller has been looking for a buyer for a long time and few bidders come forward.
